title: LNG Canada Greenlights $33B Phase 2 as Cheniere Locks Brazil Into 22-Year Deal
subhead: North American LNG took two big steps toward entrenching itself as the non-Gulf supplier of choice, while Brent climbed back above $103 after Trump ruled out sanctions relief for Iran and Treasury sanctioned another 10 entities in its 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign.

sections.heading: LNG Canada Doubles Down, Cheniere Binds Brazil for Two Decades
sections.body:
Shell and its partners gave the final investment decision on the $33-billion Phase 2 expansion of LNG Canada in Kitimat, British Columbia, according to Reuters and Canada's National Observer. The project adds two liquefaction trains and new storage, lifting capacity from 14 to 28 million tonnes per annum, with commercial operations targeted for the early 2030s. It will be fed by TC Energy's to-be-expanded 670-kilometre Coastal GasLink pipeline, which serves as the direct link from Western Canadian gas fields to the coast. Partners include PetroChina, Petronas, Mitsubishi and KOGAS. Speaking in Vancouver, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the project would connect Canadian energy to Asian and European buyers and cited it as proof of his 'one project, one review, one year' strategy; the enlarged terminal represents more than a quarter of Ottawa's goal of reaching 100 mtpa of LNG export capacity by 2040.

The same day, Cheniere Energy signed a 22-year sale and purchase agreement to supply Brazil's Petrobras with roughly 800,000 tonnes of LNG per year, on a free-on-board basis, per gCaptain. Cheniere operates Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi with about 56 mtpa combined capacity. Chairman and CEO Jack Fusco said the contract provides 'fixed-fee cash flow visibility' as the company weighs further brownfield growth.
sections.whyItMatters: Two long-dated supply commitments in one day signal that buyers and producers are increasingly pricing in years of Gulf disruption. The Gulf's share of global LNG is exactly what Hormuz risk touches, so non-Hormuz tonne capacity commands a premium. Canada is quietly converting that premium into hard infrastructure and 20-year contracts.

sections.heading: China and Asia Pull Back from Spot LNG as Prices Bite
sections.body: High prices are already reshaping demand. China's September LNG imports are on course for a second straight monthly decline, at 5.3 million tons, according to Kpler data cited by Bloomberg and reported by oilprice.com — about 8% below September 2025. Spot prices topped $26 per mmBtu in early September, roughly double a year earlier. Kpler separately forecast total Asian LNG inflows at 20.09 million tons, the lowest in eight years. Oilprice.com also reported that Chinese state importers are in talks to secure long-term supply from exporters that do not depend on the Strait of Hormuz, without cancelling binding Qatari contracts.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the demand-side mirror of the supply deals above. The world's largest LNG buyer is actively trying to de-risk its Persian Gulf exposure — a structural shift in trade flows that favors US, Canadian and other non-Gulf suppliers even after this war ends.

sections.heading: Treasury's Operation Economic Outcast Hits Iran's Military Supply Chain
sections.body: Washington escalated its economic campaign against Tehran. OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and entities across multiple jurisdictions for procuring weapons and components for Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics (MODAFL), the Treasury Department announced. Targets included a MODAFL representative in Beijing — Seyyed Asghar Alizadeh Tabatabai — and the Iran-based Kavoshcom Asia R and D Group, which sourced electronics for Iran Aircraft Manufacturing (HESA). Press accounts of the same action noted entities in China, Pakistan, Turkiye, Iran and Saudi Arabia. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the department 'will not tolerate any support to the regime.' The designations fall under Executive Order 13382 and form part of the 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign Bessent announced on August 24 and branded 'Economic D-Day.'
sections.whyItMatters: The US has shifted from strikes to supply-chain strangulation, naming third-country enablers in China, Pakistan and Turkiye. That extends the war into secondary-sanctions territory that touches US partners and creates friction with capitals the US needs for any Hormuz diplomacy.

sections.heading: Brent Back Above $103 After Trump Rules Out Sanctions Relief
sections.body: Brent crude rose 1.11% to $103.73 a barrel and WTI gained 0.38% to $89.72 by 01:30 GMT Wednesday, according to Al Jazeera via Times Now, after President Donald Trump rejected easing sanctions on Iran. Brent was set to finish September roughly 14% higher, its strongest monthly advance since July, while WTI was headed for about a 4% monthly gain. The move reversed Tuesday's losses, when oil fell as much as 2.5-3.5% on signs of Middle East export recovery. The WSJ noted that output from Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline is coming through faster than expected, and the New York Times reported more tankers moving through Hormuz as shippers regained confidence — though global supply remains below pre-war levels.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is caught between a real, partial supply recovery and political risk that refuses to resolve. The East-West pipeline carrying part of the load shows how Saudi Arabia's Red Sea bypass is absorbing stress that used to funnel entirely through Hormuz — a shift with lasting consequences for the strait's strategic weight.

sections.heading: Iran Threatens Regional Infrastructure as Hormuz Talks Drag
sections.body: Iran's chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf threatened new attacks Tuesday, saying no infrastructure in the region would be safe if Iran's security were not guaranteed, the Oman Observer reported. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in New York for the UN General Assembly, said Qatari intermediaries had 'presented ideas' on reopening the Strait and expected to convey a final US response 'by tomorrow.' Iran has maintained its blockade on commercial shipping through Hormuz since the war began in late February, while the US runs a counterblockade of Iranian ports. Fox News reported IRGC claims it still holds leverage over the strait. Araghchi separately told NBC that Iran is 'fully prepared' for renewed war 'even if it comes to a doomsday war.'
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Qatari-mediated optimism and Iranian threats to strike regional infrastructure shows the reopening is still contingent on conditions that neither side has accepted. Qatar — itself a major LNG exporter dependent on Hormuz — has become the key broker, which gives Doha unusual leverage.

sections.heading: Europe's Winter Squeeze Sharpens Over US Diesel Export Ban
sections.body: European officials are bracing for a possible US diesel export ban. The EU energy commissioner sent a letter to all 27 member states recommending they cut gas and fuel consumption, the Washington Post reported. Firstpost detailed the scale of the risk: the US produces roughly 4.8-5.1 million barrels per day of diesel and exports 1.2-1.5 million bpd, much of it to Europe, India and Latin America. Trump backed the concept on September 22 after saying the White House was reviewing it 'very seriously'; Treasury Secretary Bessent confirmed officials were weighing partial quotas or a full ban, and reports indicated a draft 90-day blanket ban was under review. US retail gasoline hit $4.48 a gallon, up $1.34 year-on-year, with ULSD inventories at 96.4 million barrels, down 14% year-on-year. Canada's energy minister told Bloomberg his country has 'backup plans' for a diesel supply disruption.
sections.whyItMatters: A US export ban would convert America's own pump-price politics into a supply shock for allies and the Global South. Europe, already facing storage levels roughly 14 percentage points below last year on some estimates, would be left scrambling for middle distillates at the worst possible moment — and the move could backfire on US refiners by forcing run cuts.

sections.heading: India Resists Russia Oil Exit as US Tariff Threat Looms
sections.body: Analysts say India will not and cannot replace its Russian crude imports despite the US threat of 100% tariffs, oilprice.com reported. The 'Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,' signed into law this month, authorizes tariffs up to 100% on large importers of Russian oil and gas. India is the second-largest importer of Russian crude after China, and Russian barrels have accounted for nearly half of Indian crude purchases in recent months. The Financial Express noted Russian flows to India could moderate somewhat as refiners explore alternatives under tariff risk, while Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal was in Washington for trade talks.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the central unresolved tension of the sanctions era: the US is asking India to pay a strategic price that New Delhi considers economically impossible to bear. The outcome will define whether Washington's secondary-sanctions architecture binds major powers or simply reroutes trade through more opacity.

bottomLine: The day's real story was structural: North America's LNG buildout hardened with LNG Canada's $33-billion FID and Cheniere's 22-year Petrobras deal, while China's state buyers began hunting for non-Hormuz supply to reduce Gulf exposure — a durable reordering of global gas trade that will outlast this war. Around the Gulf, escalation continued on the economic track: Treasury's Operation Economic Outcast named enablers in China, Pakistan and Turkiye, Trump refused Iran sanctions relief, and Brent pushed back above $103 even as Saudi's East-West pipeline let more crude flow. Iran kept threatening regional infrastructure and left Hormuz reopening contingent on conditions Washington has not accepted. The two tracks — building alternative supply and squeezing Iran's revenue — are now reinforcing each other, which suggests higher, more volatile prices persist well into the winter.
sources: Reuters, National Observer, gCaptain, oilprice.com, Bloomberg (via oilprice.com), US Treasury/OFAC, Times Now (Al Jazeera), Washington Post, Firstpost, WSJ, New York Times, Oman Observer, Fox News, Financial Express, Kpler
